speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the Ministry can carry out educational publicity to remind residents not to go to the accident and emergency departments of public hospitals except for genuine emergencies; and (b) whether the Ministry can encourage more clinics to operate on a 24-hours basis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) with the activation of inpatient teams to help at emergency departments, whether this will cause other healthcare teams to be overworked; (b) where will the manpower for transitional care facilities (TCFs), particularly the TCF with 364 beds, come from; (c) how well-equipped are healthcare workers and aides in the step-down facilities to care for transferred patients; and (d) what are the immediate measures to expand our healthcare teams, considering that some services cannot be automated in the short term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the risk of suffering from pressure injuries amongst bedridden patients who are kept for significant lengths of time at the accident and emergency departments of acute hospitals before being admitted to the wards is being monitored; and (b) whether such patients may be screened in advance for their susceptibility to develop pressure injuries and treated accordingly.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: asked the Minister for Health whether the Ministry will consider developing a gatekeeping role and process at the polyclinics and GP clinics to reduce the number of patients whose conditions do not require emergency care at hospital emergency departments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This year, as we encountered the Omicron infection waves – and we have had three so far – the pressure shifted from the ICU to the regular hospital wards, and by extension, the Emergency Departments, or EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is because Omicron is a less dangerous variant, and our population has become more resilient due to vaccinations and safe recovery from the infections.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, over the past year, I have reported to this House on several occasions that although we did not let the virus overwhelm our healthcare system, our hospitals and, especially, the EDs, have been very busy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why are the hospitals still experiencing heavy workload, given that life has gone back to pre-COVID-19 normal?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The simple and fundamental reason is that the pandemic is not over.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It may feel like it is over for most of us, but it certainly is not over for hospitals and our healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are learning to live with the virus, as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have explained to the House before, endemicity does not mean the virus disappears from our lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the contrary, it means that it is a permanent feature of our lives, circulating amongst us and we have to take personal precautions and implement public health measures in order to manage and live with it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, the safe management measures (SMMs) to restrict social interactions and, therefore, reduce viral transmission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Two, transmission still happens and, therefore, we do vaccinations, so that infections do not translate into many cases of severe illnesses and deaths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When these two cannot prevent cases, the third lever – which is our healthcare system – will then have to manage; it has to catch the problem and then, manage it by treating and caring for infected patients who become severely ill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Let us take stock of the three measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For SMMs, we have removed almost all restrictions, so that life goes back to the pre-COVID-19 normal.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is what all Singaporeans wish for and the whole point of treating COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, the Multi-Ministry Taskforce (MTF) has been very reluctant to re-impose SMMs, unless it is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have already covered the great majority – over 90% – of our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our vaccination exercise is ongoing, but this is largely to extend our coverage at the margins, namely, now, infants and very young children, and to keep vaccinations up-to-date for the others.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are just maintaining our immunity and resilience, now no longer able to achieve the kind of quantum improvement in resilience that we could achieve when we first started our national vaccination programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means that the burden of endemicity will fall disproportionately on the last public health measure – which is our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why our wards and EDs have been very busy over the past year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The media highlighted it only recently, but really, our hospitals have been experiencing it for the whole year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I hope that as we enjoy our hard-fought freedom from COVID-19, we remember the toil and sacrifice of our healthcare workers – doctors, nurses, social care workers and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are sacrificing and toiling away, in order to secure freedom and the state of endemicity for the rest of society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, COVID-19 may feel like it is over for many of us; it is not over for them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the hospitals and EDs, therefore, service levels may drop and waiting times become longer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Out of frustration, we understand that there will be public complaints, but I sincerely hope that our hospitals and healthcare workers will continue to receive the appreciation, understanding and support of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, I want to assure the House, that for critically ill patients, they are attended to almost immediately at the EDs, due to the way that we triage patients and allocate resources.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not a very long wait, and it is important for this group of patients to be attended to quickly, so that they are evaluated and then can be discharged promptly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Despite the heavy workload, our hospitals will not compromise the safety of patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As mentioned earlier, life-threatening cases will be attended to immediately.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If surgery is required, it will be carried out promptly and beds will be there for the patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For non-life-threatening patients who are waiting for admission, medical teams will continue to monitor them and institute appropriate investigations and treatments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For bedridden patients who are at higher risk of developing pressure injuries, hospitals will implement preventive nursing interventions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This includes the use of thicker mattresses or air mattresses, turning of the patients periodically and changing of diapers and drawsheets for bedridden patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it has not been easy to solve the problem as we are still in the middle of a pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Each time a wave subsides and we started dealing with the problem, another wave would come, and attention and resources will be diverted to fight fire again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With the XBB wave subsiding earlier than expected, we hope that this time round, we will have the time and space to deal with the problem properly and decisively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To do so, we need to diagnose where exactly is the operational bottleneck.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is really about matching the demand and supply of hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The crowdedness and long waiting times for patients at the EDs in some hospitals, especially during a wave, is a manifestation of the problem, a mismatch of demand and supply of hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Let us look at the demand for hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, translated to daily attendances, it was about 2,500 patients a day in 2019 to 2,100 patients a day in 2022.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, it would appear that all of our measures to educate the public to not go to EDs unless absolutely necessary, the GPFirst initiative and the setting up Urgent Care Centres in the heartlands as an alternative – they have all worked.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In absolute numbers, this is an increase of a few hundred patients per month.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not huge but it does add to the operational burden of hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, I think, is this point, we are again looking at averages.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While the average number has come down, during a pandemic, that number is a lot more volatile.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, during an infection wave, many more infected people and recovered patients go to EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is 30% more workload at the ED, which is very significant.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should mention a separate problem that we now encounter at KK Women's and Children's Hospital (KKH).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The ED has been experiencing very high visits every day – at levels that they used to experience only during Chinese New Year, when all other clinics are closed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, come Chinese New Year this round, I do not know what kind of numbers they are going to get.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a separate problem, due to what we call an "immunity debt" in children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means that for the past two years, SMMs – including mask wearing – has shielded children from many forms of viral infection, and not just COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Now that life is back to normal, viral infections are making a strong comeback and demanding payback – with interest!

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Let us look at the supply side of the hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a few factors constraining the supply and slowing down the process of warding ED patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, due to our ageing population, there is a secular trend of rising numbers of patients with long stays and that reduces the turnover of hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, the pandemic caused construction disruptions which delayed the opening of healthcare facilities, namely the Woodlands Health Campus and the Integrated Care Hub at Tan Tock Seng Hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If these facilities had opened as originally planned in 2022 without the COVID-19-related delays, they would have added at least a few hundred beds to our system and would have alleviated the problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Similarly, construction delays due to the pandemic have also postponed the opening of several nursing homes and community day care facilities, and that also constrained the ability of hospitals to discharge less acute patients and free up hospital beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As part of our emergency planning, hospitals are required now to set aside, or ringfence, beds for the care of COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members of the House may recall at the height of the pandemic – and at that time we were imposing SMMs to preserve healthcare capacity – many Parliamentary Questions were filed, asking the Ministry of Health (MOH) if we had planned for adequate healthcare capacity in such emergency scenarios.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Well, ringfencing hospital beds for COVID-19 patients is part of that planning effort.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: About 80% were occupied at the peak of the wave, which meant we still had 160 beds unoccupied for contingency purposes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Not a big number, but nevertheless, constrains hospital operations and impedes the clearing of patients waiting at EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether due to demand or supply factors, we need to recognise this – that is, we run a very high throughput hospital system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In such a system, even a very small mismatch of demand and supply, a couple of hundred beds, will cause waiting times to spike up very significantly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You think of it that way – it is not very different from an expressway with very heavy traffic flow.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All it needs is for one branch to fall on one lane or half a lane, and you will have a massive traffic jam.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have a similar situation in a very high throughput hospital system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, how do we resolve the current problem?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The hospital clusters, working with MOH, have issued a statement recently, outlining all the measures they are taking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They continue to be relevant and we will continue to pursue them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Just to briefly recap, they include the reducing of EDs demand through primary care, alternative pre-hospital care options; educating the public to use EDs only when absolutely necessary; diverting them to nearby primary care clinics; and coordinating with the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) to divert less serious cases away to less crowded EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are also actively transferring patients in acute hospitals to step down or home care whenever possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are partnering private hospitals, such as Raffles Hospital, to accept patients sent by SCDF ambulances for emergency medical treatment and we also offer subsidised rates even though treatment is at Raffles Hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: New nursing homes are coming on stream and they are very helpful during the XBB wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From the end of next year, Woodlands Health Campus and Tan Tock Seng Hospital Integrated Care Hub should start to open progressively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But today, let me focus on two important structural adjustments that we will make which will hopefully help to alleviate the crowdedness at EDs in the short term.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are operated by private providers at wards at Sengkang Community Hospital, Changi Expo Hall 10 and Crawfurd Hospital, along Farrer Road, which just opened a few days ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They admit medically stable patients from public hospitals while they wait for their transfers to intermediate or long-term care facilities, or for their discharge plans to be finalised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is, therefore, a very important step-down care facility, to free up acute beds in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But TCFs are not just about providing beds space that is operated by private hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There has to be a very firm handshake between the TCF operator and a public hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because with that firm handshake, the privately operated TCF will gain confidence in admitting patients transferred by a public hospital – because they will feel assured that should they need any clinical help, in unforseen circumstances and for some complications, the public hospital will still step in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Without this understanding, TCFs will naturally be very conservative in admitting patients and there will be very little movement in stable patients.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Sengkang Community Hospital TCF run by Thomson Medical Centre is a very good example.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have a very strong partnership now with Sengkang General Hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will replicate this, to pair up Changi General Hospital with Expo Hall 10 run by Raffles Medical Group; and Tan Tock Seng Hospital with Crawfurd Hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are actively working on new TCFs in the north and in the west, to partner Khoo Teck Puat Hospital and Ng Teng Fong General Hospital respectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second structural shift: our approach to living with COVID-19 needs to be extended to hospital operations as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We had done so in the earlier stages of the pandemic, when hospitalised COVID-19 patients faced a very high chance of developing severe illnesses and numbers can spike very high during an infection wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, reserving beds – actually, we reserved wards – is the appropriate thing to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we are now at the stage when most residents have been vaccinated and boosted or recovered safely from COVID-19 and have good levels of hybrid immunity against severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should, therefore, allow hospitals to triage or assess their patients based on clinical severity and priority for treatment, and not manage COVID-19 patients to a different standard.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This flexibility is important for our hospitals to help them optimise the use of beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In a crunch situation, just like the expressway with very high throughput, it makes all the difference.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With this change, hospitals will no longer set aside whole wards to cohort COVID-19 positive patients as a standard pandemic practice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will continue their current practice of using isolation beds for patients with infectious diseases, including COVID-19, if there is a risk of infection spread.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not a sudden change, but a transition process that has started and is ongoing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hospitals will continue to exercise various precautionary measures on infection control to protect the vulnerable and prevent spreading of infectious diseases in hospitals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have done so for many years, for influenza, for all kinds of infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will apply the same measures now for COVID-19, but without setting aside entire wards which will stall their operations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Beyond these two structural measures, every one of us can do our part.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Use alternatives, such a general practitioner (GP) clinic or call our family doctors.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should exercise social responsibility, such as staying at home and self-testing when not feeling well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most importantly, we need to continue to keep our vaccinations up-to-date and prevent ourselves from falling severely ill if we are infected by COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: One is, what is the estimated backlog of —

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the estimated backlog for elective surgeries that we are currently facing now?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: And what is MOH doing now about this and when we clear this backlog?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because ever since we started opening up, hospitals have all realised that to postpone electives and postpone non-urgent surgery, it all comes back after a while – and with interest usually.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, for the past two or three waves, we have been very reluctant to postpone these electives.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Earlier this year, my 90-year-old mother was ill and I just found it so difficult to find a 24-hour clinic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if MOH can encourage more clinics to open for longer hours, that will certainly help.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Otherwise, my option was to send her to the emergency department.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The second question, Sir, is TCFs, will that be a difference in cost because these would be run by private clinics?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if I am a patient going to a TCF, I would be concerned about the cost.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And finally, what is the percentage of space that is available, when you free up the number of beds for COVID-19 purposes?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The short answer is we will try to encourage it, but opening for 24 hours is not easy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They will need a few doctors to cover each other.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many clinics do open to late at night and, hopefully, with something like Healthier SG, we are changing the mindset of GPs and also changing health-seeking behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hopefully, we will get more help from GPs in attending to some of these urgent cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For your mother, if it is in the middle of the night, I think going to ED is probably justified.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are running these and subsidising them in the same way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think they will make a big difference to the operation of hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, I am heartened to hear that TCFs will be paired with our hospitals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, would there be enough healthcare workers to run the TCFs, given the overall tightened manpower situation in our hospitals?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, how is MOH supporting our healthcare workers to do their work more efficiently and to prevent burnout during this period of high patient load?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We know that healthcare workers are never enough.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is a manpower crunch and intense competition between different countries trying to hire healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, this is something we are doing actively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Now that the COVID-19 situation has stabilised, borders are opening up, we have started our overseas recruitment process as well as continue to work with our local institutions to bring in more healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second question on how to prevent burnout, if we solve all these jam problems, manage the pandemic and move to endemicity form of operations, I think it will go a great extent to reduce the workload.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I deeply appreciate all our healthcare workers and staff – from doctors to nurses to hospital receptionists – for their tireless efforts in caring for patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Both they and the patients suffer tremendous stress when the queues of patients build up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, I have two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, I understand that some patients are not discharged because the downstream care facilities are not available to receive and accommodate them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said just now that there were some delays in the opening of nursing homes and daycare facilities, and transitional care facilities are being used to reduce the burden on acute care hospitals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry also look into providing more home support for patients to help their families care for the patients who are suitable for discharge from acute care hospitals?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, queue clearance depends, in part, on the ability to triage and diagnose arriving patients and this, in turn, is limited by the number of qualified healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry looking at giving greater responsibilities to nurses so that they can take on more of the responsibilities that are currently being done by doctors?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are certainly looking at home discharge as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in a complex system like that, it is all of the above – whether it is a nursing home, step-down care, community hospital, home discharge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Just a point on home discharge: actually, it is quite manpower intensive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because once you bring a patient home, a nurse does have to visit them, call them; but it frees up the bed spaces.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it does add to the workload of nurses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are managing different resources as optimally as we can.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But this is a major area that, at some point, we should discuss further with Healthier SG, ageing-in-place, home nursing is a very important prong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, on triage, I think nurses are already doing some of the triaging.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And certainly, with our move to Healthier SG, preventive care, bringing healthcare into the community away from the hospitals, there is a lot more our nurses, allied health professionals and pharmacists can do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a direction we are moving towards.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also want to express my deep appreciation to our healthcare workers, especially the doctors, nurses and staff working in the EDs, some of whom are my personal friends and I have seen how they have persevered through these few years of COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My second supplementary question is that I have spoken to some of the GPs in my Jalan Kayu constituency about the situation in the EDs and what is the role that they can play, especially under Healthier SG to be part of the solution for the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have asked whether there can be more practical resources, such as a peer-to-peer call line for them to reach out to their Accident and Emergency (A&E) doctor counterparts in the public hospitals in the region so that they can triage and also assure the patients that the conditions may not warrant an ED admission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First question, I do not have the number.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Maybe the Member can file another Parliamentary Question?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: GPs can certainly take a load off the EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, open 24 hours; if not, open at night, make yourself available to telemedicine; you can assuage the concerns of many patients and avoid the ED visits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have one supplementary question for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There may be elderly facing non-life-threatening cases who may not have been able to share their condition while waiting for a doctor to see them at the A&E.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may have felt nauseous, cold, scared, hungry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How then does MOH identify or how then do the nurses identify such cases and help comfort them during that waiting period?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When the queue is long and you start to have crowded EDs, the nurses do that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think they have the skills to do that, including the language ability, because in a team, there will be multiple language skills and they would be able to comfort the elderly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the problem that the Member raised is probably a result of very crowded EDs, when nurses are under tremendous pressure, so the kind of attention is probably not given, compared to normal times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think we still go back to the same problem we raised earlier, that if we can resolve the crowdedness at the EDs, I think the problem that the Member raised will be addressed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Minister mentioned about the non-urgent cases attended by EDs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand some are because the clinics could not cope and refer the patients to EDs – including some polyclinics, I understand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I ask the Minister – he mentioned about TCF, whether that can also be another place?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can clinics refer patients to a TCF instead of going to the EDs?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have one in Admiralty and that has been very useful.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ultimately, it goes back to how we diagnose a problem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Reducing non-emergency cases to EDs certainly will help.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But that is not the main bottleneck today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The main bottleneck remains a mismatch in demand and supply of hospital beds, which leads to long waiting times at the EDs, waiting for wards and crowding the EDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, that remains the most urgent problem to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a question on the situation at KKH.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister spoke about the heavy demand on beds there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister have some indication as to when that demand is likely to taper or is it a case of having to stand up more beds in KKH over time?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The bed situation for paediatrics is actually quite okay.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a different problem from the EDs of the other hospitals where there is a mismatch in demand and supply of beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is more a case of ED visits, where they can be attended to, treated and discharged and go home.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned there is an immunity debt, which means it can be repaid over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As to how long – I have to consult the experts in MOH, and they may have some idea.
